source.title_on_document: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students' essays.

paper_design_summary: Eighteen second-year master's students in forensic sciences at the University of Split volunteered to write an 800 to 1000 word essay in Croatian on biometric identification in forensic sciences, with up to four hours. The authors divided them into two groups of nine, balanced on study module and GPA; one group used ChatGPT and the other wrote traditionally under supervision. Two teachers graded the essays with a rubric (mechanics, style, content, format; A to D), and the authors also measured writing time, PlagScan unauthenticity, pairwise Jaccard similarity between essays, and an AI text classifier label.

studies.label: Essay writing with or without ChatGPT (forensic sciences master's students)

assignment.what_was_assigned: ChatGPT assistance (experimental group) versus traditional essay writing without ChatGPT (control group)
assignment.quote: we divided them into two groups according to the study module (Crime Scene Investigation, Forensic Chemistry and Molecular Biology, and Forensics and National Security) and the weighted grade point average (GPA) to ensure the similar composition of the groups.

arms.name: Experimental (GPT)
arms.description: Wrote the essay with ChatGPT assistance after an introduction to the tool; GPA = 3.92 ± 0.57

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Wrote the essay traditionally, supervised to make sure they did not use ChatGPT; GPA = 3.92 ± 0.46

participants.exclusions: None reported. Self-selection into the study: 18 of the 50 students enrolled in the course applied by web form.
participants.who: Second-year master's students, University Department of Forensic Sciences, University of Split, enrolled in the course Forensic sciences seminar
participants.quote: Out of 50 students enrolled in the course, 18 applied by web form and participated in the study.
participants.locator: p. 2, Materials and methods; arm sizes p. 2-3 ('The control group (n = 9 ...' and 'the experimental group (n = 9 ...') and p. 1, Abstract

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT ('ChatGTP assistance, version 2.1.0'); called ChatGPT-3 in this preprint and ChatGPT-3.5 in the journal title
ai_tool.how_used: Experimental group was introduced to ChatGPT and used it as a writing assistant during the essay session; no further restrictions described.

task.description: Expository essay of 800 to 1000 words in Croatian, title 'The advantages and disadvantages of biometric identification in forensics sciences', Vancouver citation style; graded for mechanics, style, content, and format, not for creativity.
task.duration: Up to four hours; students could leave when they wanted (mean 172.22 ± 31.59 min GPT, 179.11 ± 31.93 min control, p. 4)

outcomes.name: Essay score (mean of four rubric grades, A=4 to D=1)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: control (2.39 ± 0.71) vs GTP group (2.00 ± 0.73), n = 9 each; linear regression on group, writing duration, module, GPA: group (P = 0.184)
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Results; Figure 1A p. 5; abstract p. 1

diversity_detail.metric: Jaccard similarity index, calculated using the R package Textreuse (PDF p. 3, Materials and methods).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not applicable to this lexical measure; no embedding model is used.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of essays across the whole sample, including within-control, within-GPT, and between-group pairs (Control1-Control9 and GPT1-GPT9; PDF p. 6, Supplementary table 1).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No arm-level standard error, confidence interval, or comparison test is reported (PDF p. 4, Results; p. 6, Supplementary table 1).
diversity_detail.notes: Pooled-sample median Jaccard similarity index 0.002 (0 – 0.054) (PDF p. 4, Results). Supplementary table 1 reports individual pairwise values (PDF p. 6). The authors describe no remarkable similarities between essays regardless of ChatGPT use (PDF p. 7, Discussion). No arm-level similarity summary or test is reported, so no between-group contrast or direction is coded. The number of analyzed pairs is not explicitly reported, so n_units remains null.

contrasts.reported: The mean of text unauthenticity was 11.87% ±13.45 in the GPT-assisted group and 9.96% ± 9.81% in the control group (no test reported)

eligibility.reason: Core eligibility remains no. Criterion 2 is not met: 18 people were analyzed (9 GPT, 9 control; PDF p. 1, Abstract; pp. 2-3, Materials and methods), below the 50-person threshold. Criterion 1 remains unclear: the authors divided volunteers into groups balanced on study module and GPA without stating random assignment (PDF p. 2, Materials and methods); randomized counts remain null. Criterion 3 is met because pairwise Jaccard similarity is computed on essays produced by different participants (PDF p. 3, Materials and methods; p. 4, Results; p. 6, Supplementary table 1), meeting the output-diversity criterion in creativity-codebook.md sections 1 and 3. The absence of an arm-level similarity summary or test limits contrast extraction. The documented quasi_people design belongs in observational context under creativity-codebook.md sections 3-4 and the form-spec.md design_class field note.

one_line_finding: With 9 students per group, ChatGPT-assisted essays scored no higher than control essays (2.00 ± 0.73 vs 2.39 ± 0.71; group P = 0.184) and between-essay Jaccard similarity was low overall (median 0.002, range 0 to 0.054), with no arm-level similarity contrast reported (p. 4, Results).
